aboutPage.title: Substrate — About
aboutPage.description: The story behind Substrate: why we exist, the statements that govern every engagement, the people accountable for them, and the record so far.
aboutPage.label: About Substrate
aboutPage.heading: Built to be built on.
aboutPage.lede: Who we are and how we work: the story behind the company, the statements that govern every engagement, the people accountable for them, and the record so far.

paragraphs: Substrate was founded in 2016 by engineers who kept getting the same phone call — after launch day, when the platform that demoed beautifully met production traffic and cracked. We had spent years inside those systems, and the diagnosis rarely changed: the visible product was fine; the layer beneath it was improvised.

So we built a company for that layer. The name comes from geology — the substrate is the stratum everything above rests on — and it set the standard for the work: foundations are not glamorous, but nothing stands without them. We architect before we code, write the decisions down, and ship systems designed to be operated, not just launched.
A decade on, that is still the whole business: cloud platforms, data systems, and AI-native software for organizations that cannot afford to be wrong about their foundations.
story.pullQuote: Nothing we build is the thing you see. It's the reason the thing you see stands.

scale.label: Engineering at Scale
scale.title: Systems designed to run for a decade, not a demo.
scale.lede: We treat every engagement as infrastructure. The diagram below is how we think: clear layers, explicit contracts, and data that flows through systems built to carry it.

points.title: Architecture before code
points.body: Every system begins as a set of explicit decisions — boundaries, contracts, failure modes, and scale envelopes — recorded before the first commit.

points.title: Instrumented from day one
points.body: Observability is designed in, not bolted on. Platforms we build explain themselves in production: traces, metrics, and budgets from the first release.

points.title: Built to be operated
points.body: We engineer for the team that runs the system. Automation, runbooks, and SLOs ship with the platform — because launch day is the beginning.

process.label: Process
process.title: No mysteries. A cadence you can plan around.
process.lede: Five phases, one shape: understand before designing, design before building, and never hand over a system we wouldn't operate ourselves.

phases.title: Discover
phases.body: We map the terrain before we drill: stakeholders, systems, constraints, and the metrics that will define success — in your words, then in numbers.
phases.glyphAlt: Sketch: contour survey with a marked drill site

phases.title: Architect
phases.body: Explicit decisions, recorded: boundaries, contracts, failure modes. The target architecture is reviewed with your engineers, not presented to them.
phases.glyphAlt: Sketch: a floor plan with a dimension line

phases.title: Build
phases.body: Vertical slices to production from the first sprint. Working software is the status report; everything else is commentary.
phases.glyphAlt: Sketch: a trunk-based git graph with a merge commit

phases.title: Harden
phases.body: Load modeling, security review, chaos drills. We try to break the system before your customers get the chance.
phases.glyphAlt: Sketch: a load spike chart guarded by a shield

phases.title: Operate
phases.body: We run what we build — then teach your team to run it without us. Success is our pager going quiet.
phases.glyphAlt: Sketch: an uptime trace and a handover arrow

work.label: Work
work.title: Shipped, measured, and still running.
work.lede: Client names stay behind NDAs; the numbers don't. Three engagements, reported the way we report them internally — what was broken, what we built, what changed.

cases.title: The payments core came off the mainframe without missing a settlement window.
cases.body: A tier-one bank ran its payment rails on a core older than most of its engineers. We built the replacement beside it, mirrored six months of production traffic through both, and reconciled every transaction until the diff was zero. Then we cut over — one weekend, no missed windows.
cases.figCaption: FIG. 06.1 — SETTLEMENT LATENCY, BEFORE AND AFTER CUTOVER
cases.figAlt: Chart: p99 settlement time holding near 4.2 seconds, then dropping to 180 milliseconds at the week-26 cutover

cases.title: A national delivery network that replans itself every ninety seconds.
cases.body: A national parcel carrier planned routes overnight, in batch — by morning the plan was already wrong. We replaced it with a streaming optimizer that replans the entire network every ninety seconds and reroutes drivers mid-shift, using the traffic and load data it just watched happen.
cases.figCaption: FIG. 06.2 — LIVE REPLANNING TOPOLOGY, ONE HUB OF NINE
cases.figAlt: Diagram: a routing hub continuously dispatching to depots and ports, with live route pulses

cases.title: Four thousand substations, one source of truth.
cases.body: A utility's substations reported into eleven systems that didn't agree with each other. We consolidated grid telemetry onto one streaming platform — every reading queryable within seconds of hitting the wire, and clean enough to retrain the load forecasts that had been quietly drifting for years.
cases.figCaption: FIG. 06.3 — TELEMETRY INGEST RAMP, FIRST YEAR
cases.figAlt: Chart: telemetry ingest volume climbing through the first year, with a dashed forecast continuing past today

contactFAQ.heading: Frequently asked questions
contactFAQ.lede: Enterprise buyers evaluate engineering partners thoroughly. These are the questions we hear most often.

items.q: How quickly will I hear back after submitting an inquiry?
items.a: Our team aims to respond within two working days. The reply comes from an engineer in the relevant practice area, not from a sales representative.

items.q: What happens after I submit the contact form?
items.a: Your inquiry is reviewed by the relevant practice lead. If there is a clear fit, we schedule a discovery call. If your needs fall outside our expertise, we will tell you directly.

items.q: Do I need a detailed brief before contacting you?
items.a: No. A high-level description of your situation is sufficient to start the conversation. We will help you scope the details during the discovery process.

items.q: How does Substrate charge for engagements?
items.a: We provide fixed-price proposals for well-scoped projects and team-based pricing for ongoing engagements. All pricing is transparent and itemized. We do not charge markup on contractor rates.

items.q: Can we sign an NDA before discussing our project?
items.a: Yes. We routinely sign NDAs before discovery conversations. We treat every client's information as confidential from the first contact.

items.q: Do you work with international clients?
items.a: Yes. We deliver services across North America, Europe, and Asia-Pacific. Our global delivery model allows us to staff engagements with the right engineers regardless of geography.

We collaborate asynchronously by default using tools your team already uses: Slack, Teams, GitHub, Jira, or similar. We schedule synchronous working sessions for architecture discussions and sprint ceremonies.

items.q: What does project onboarding look like?
items.a: Engagements begin with a kickoff week: environment access, knowledge transfer sessions, tooling setup, and the first sprint planning. We aim to deliver value by the end of week one.

items.q: Do you provide ongoing support after a project?
items.a: Yes. Many clients transition from project delivery to managed operations or retainer-based advisory. We structure engagement transitions to match your operational needs.

items.q: What technology stacks do you work with?
items.a: We are proficient across AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes, Terraform, TypeScript, Python, Go, Rust, PostgreSQL, Kafka, and modern AI/ML stacks. Our full technology ecosystem is documented on our capabilities page.
A structured working session where we map your current state, identify constraints, define success metrics, and agree on a target architecture. It typically runs one to three days.

Yes. Architecture reviews are one of our most common engagement types. We review your existing systems, identify risks and improvement opportunities, and provide a written report with actionable recommendations.

items.q: What size enterprise engagements do you handle?
items.a: We work with organizations from growth-stage startups to Fortune 500 enterprises. Engagement sizes range from two-week advisory sprints to multi-year platform programs with distributed teams.

items.q: How do you handle data security and compliance?
items.a: Security is integrated into our engineering process from day one. We design for SOC 2, GDPR, HIPAA, PCI-DSS, and FedRAMP requirements where applicable. Data residency and sovereignty are treated as architectural constraints.

items.q: Can you work alongside our existing engineering team?
items.a: Yes. We commonly work embedded within client engineering organizations. Our engineers integrate into your existing workflows, attend your ceremonies, and collaborate directly with your team.

items.q: What is the typical engagement duration?
items.a: Engagements range from short-term advisory (two to six weeks) to multi-year platform partnerships. We prefer longer engagements because deep understanding produces better outcomes.
